subject: english-language
topicDisplay: Unit 1: Writing for Purpose and Audience and Reading to Access Non-fiction and Media Texts
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Section A: Writing for Purpose and Audience
Writing accurately: spelling, punctuation and grammar
Section B: Reading to Access Non-Fiction and Media Texts
Analysing language, persuasive and presentational devices

questions.q: Which purpose describes writing that is designed to make the reader agree with a particular point of view?
questions.explain: Persuasive writing aims to win the reader over to a viewpoint or course of action.

questions.q: When planning a piece of non-fiction writing, the three key factors a writer must consider are usually summarised as purpose, audience and:
questions.explain: Purpose, audience and form (PAF) together shape the choices a writer makes.

questions.q: Which language choice is most appropriate when writing for an audience of young children?
options: Complex subordinate clauses and technical jargon
questions.explain: Matching vocabulary and sentence length to the audience keeps the text accessible to young readers.

questions.q: You are writing a letter to your headteacher to request a change to school uniform policy. Which register is most suitable?
questions.explain: A formal request to a figure of authority calls for a polite, formal register.

questions.q: Which persuasive technique groups three words or ideas together for emphasis and rhythm?
questions.explain: The rule of three uses a set of three items to make a point memorable and emphatic.

questions.q: What is the main effect of using a rhetorical question in persuasive writing?
options: It prompts the reader to think and draws them towards the writer's viewpoint
It provides the exact statistics needed to prove a point
It signals the end of a paragraph
It gives a neutral, factual description
questions.explain: A rhetorical question needs no answer but nudges the reader to agree with the writer.

questions.q: Why might a writer use direct address ('you') in a persuasive text?
options: To make the reader feel personally involved and spoken to
To hide the writer's opinion entirely
To make the text more formal and impersonal
To provide a bibliography of sources
questions.explain: Direct address speaks to the reader personally, increasing engagement and involvement.

questions.q: Which of the following is a presentational device rather than a language device?
questions.explain: Presentational devices such as subheadings affect layout and appearance, not word choice.

questions.q: What is the purpose of emotive language in a persuasive or media text?
options: To provoke a strong emotional response in the reader
questions.explain: Emotive language chooses words that stir feelings, making the reader more receptive to the argument.

questions.q: You want to persuade readers to recycle more. Which sentence uses a statistic for persuasive effect?
options: Over 90% of household waste can actually be recycled.
Recycling is quite a nice thing to do.
Please just have a think about it sometime.
The bins outside are coloured green.
questions.explain: A precise statistic lends authority and evidence to the persuasive point.

questions.q: In a non-fiction text, a statement that can be proved true is best described as a:
questions.explain: A fact is a statement that can be verified as true, unlike an opinion.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is an opinion rather than a fact?
options: This is the most exciting book you will ever read.
questions.explain: A judgement such as 'most exciting' expresses a viewpoint that cannot be proved, so it is an opinion.

questions.q: An account of a person's life written by that person themselves is called a(n):
questions.explain: An autobiography is a life story told by the person who lived it.

questions.q: A factual account of a person's life written by another person is called a:
questions.explain: A biography is a life story written about someone by another author.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a headline in a newspaper or media text?
options: To grab attention and summarise the story
To provide a full list of references
To give the writer's home address
questions.explain: A headline is designed to catch the reader's eye and signal what the article is about.

questions.q: What are the two main uses of an apostrophe in English?
options: To show possession and to mark omitted letters in contractions
To end a sentence and to open a quotation
To join two main clauses and to make a list
To indicate a question and to add emphasis
questions.explain: Apostrophes show ownership (the dog's bowl) and mark missing letters (do not to don't).

questions.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: The students' books were left in the classroom.
The students books were left in the classroom's.
The student's books' were left in the classroom.
The students books' were left in the classroom.
questions.explain: For a plural noun ending in -s, the possessive apostrophe goes after the -s (students').

questions.q: In an argument, what does the connective 'furthermore' signal to the reader?
options: That an additional supporting point is being added
That a contrasting idea is coming next
That the writer is reaching a conclusion
questions.explain: 'Furthermore' is an additive connective that builds on the previous point.

questions.q: A personal blog aimed at teenagers is most likely to use:
options: An informal, chatty register with personal anecdotes
Dense technical terminology with no personal voice
The passive voice throughout to sound objective
questions.explain: An informal register and personal anecdotes suit the relaxed, conversational form of a teen blog.

questions.q: Which opening would work best for a persuasive speech encouraging students to exercise more?
options: A rhetorical question that directly addresses the audience
A long list of technical medical statistics
A formal dictionary definition of the word 'exercise'
A neutral factual report on local sports facilities
questions.explain: A rhetorical question with direct address immediately engages listeners and draws them in.
